title: Inconvenient Human Rights: Access to Water and Sanitation in Sweden's Informal Roma Settlements
rationale: The record directly examines access to water and sanitation in informal Roma settlements in Sweden (Criterion 1 & Criterion 4) and focuses on municipal eviction enforcement, informal tenure, and legal/administrative obligations to provide alternative water and sanitation access (Criterion 2 narrow and plain). Although the abstract cites empirical figures ('more than 80 evictions ... between 2013 and 2016') from a multi-university socio-legal report, it does not explicitly describe primary empirical data-collection methods versus doctrinal human rights analysis (Criterion 3 unclear). Per Phase 5 rules against prematurely excluding socio-legal and informal-settlement studies, the record is marked 'unsure' for full-text verification.

title: Integrated governance for equitable water access in informal settlements in Indian cities
rationale: This empirical mixed-methods study (household surveys, stakeholder interviews, and water quality assessments across 34 slum areas in Hyderabad, India) clearly meets Criteria 1, 3, and 4 regarding household/community drinking water access disparities and uneven service delivery in informal settlements. Because the abstract frames the exposure broadly around governance dimensions, decision-making frameworks, and institutional and economic dimensions without specifying whether specific legal/administrative rule-types (such as slum notification/tenure rules, connection eligibility, tariffs/subsidies, or utility regulatory mandates) are analysed in the full text, it is retained as 'unsure' under the narrow Criterion 2 reading rather than prematurely excluded.

title: “We Are All Sick”: Sanitation, Structural Neglect, and the Embodied Politics of Informality in Cape Town
rationale: This qualitative empirical study (interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists in Khayelitsha, Cape Town) directly examines household/community sanitation access outcomes (open toilets, bucket disposal, inadequate service provision) and explicitly links inadequate provision to an administrative/tenure classification mechanism (authorities' continued classification of the settlement as 'temporary' and conditional treatment of urban infrastructure entitlements). All eligibility criteria (C1-C4) are clearly satisfied at the Title/Abstract stage.

title: Slum living conditions vary from one country to another, and subsequently within those countries from one settlement to another.
rationale: The provided title and abstract (which appear to be a truncated opening excerpt with footnotes from the article body) clearly address household and community water and sanitation infrastructure and network connections in slums/informal settlements (c1 = yes, c4 = yes). It references tenure insecurity, absence of plot/resident information, government planning, and whether infrastructure expansion is authorised and financed, making a narrow legal/administrative/tenure/utility-governance mechanism plausible (c2_narrow = unclear, c2_plain = unclear). Because the excerpt cuts off mid-sentence in the introductory discussion, whether the full paper presents empirical primary evidence or a systematic synthesis versus a non-empirical review cannot be determined without full-text inspection (c3 = unclear). Per Phase 5 rules against prematurely excluding ambiguous informal-settlement water/sanitation records, full-text retrieval is required ('unsure').

title: Rainwater Treatment in Informal Settlements with a One Health Approach and Community Service Learning: Case Study of San Isidro Patios, Bogotá, Colombia
authors: Camilo Alberto Torres Parra; Yelinca Saldeño Madero; Juan José Castiblanco-Prieto; Camila Jaramillo Monroy; Mauricio González Méndez; Alejandro Ángel Torres; Noé Villegas Flóres
rationale: Although the project addresses household/community drinking water shortages in an informal settlement in Bogotá (C1/C4), the exposure/intervention is purely technical and pedagogical project delivery—designing and implementing a rainwater harvesting and treatment system alongside One Health service-learning education—with no examination of legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, or tariff mechanisms governing service access (fails C2; E03).

title: Women In Slum Risking Their Safety To Access And Usage Of Basic Water And Sanitation Facilities
authors: Ayush Prakash Hazare; Jyoti Jain Tholiya
rationale: Although the record concerns community water and sanitation facilities (public toilets and common toilet complexes) in slums (C1 met) and barriers to safe access/use (C4 plausibly met), the explanatory factors explicitly identified in the abstract are physical, spatial, and infrastructural (lighting, location, route, toilet block infrastructure, and number of toilets) driving gender-based violence and crime against women, with no legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or institutional governance mechanism examined (fails C2; primary exclusion code E03). It is also unclear from the abstract whether the paper reports primary empirical data or a general narrative overview (C3 unclear).

title: The Regulation of Private Sector Participation in Urban Water Supply and Sanitation: Realising Social and Environmental Objectives in Developing Countries
authors: Nick Johnstone; Wood, Libby; Robert R. Hearne
rationale: The study clearly addresses urban water supply and sanitation service provision (C1) and regulatory mechanisms governing private sector participation, customer protection, and basic service-level guarantees (C2 narrow and plain). However, from the abstract's reference to 'a review of five case studies' providing 'an overview of the issues involved and some of the mechanisms available', full-text inspection is needed to determine whether it reports primary empirical case-study evidence or a non-systematic policy overview (C3) and whether household/community service access outcomes are empirically evaluated (C4).

title: Water reuse in Africa: challenges and opportunities
authors: Aki√ßa Bahri; Pay Drechsel; François Brissaud
rationale: Excluded (E07 wrong service, also failing C2 narrow, C3 empirical design and C4 access outcome). The paper is a high-level regional policy and conceptual overview focused on urban/peri-urban wastewater reuse for informal agricultural irrigation and health-risk reduction at places of reuse in Africa, rather than an empirical study or systematic review of legal or administrative mechanisms governing household or community water or sanitation service access.

title: Kampala’s Heterogeneous Sanitation Infrastructures: Exemplars of Survival and Disruption
rationale: This qualitative empirical study (in-depth interviews, critical observation, and systematic literature review) examines private, shared, and communal informal sanitation modalities across Kampala's faecal sludge service chain and documents disparities in sanitation deficiency among the urban poor (meeting C1, C3, and C4). Because the abstract highlights informality, multi-actor working arrangements involving public institutions, planning/policy discourse, and the need for formal recognition and governance reform without specifying which concrete legal, regulatory, licensing, tenure, or tariff rules are empirically analysed, full-text retrieval is required under the narrow Criterion 2 reading ('unsure').

title: Synergies and Trade-offs between Sanitation and the Sustainable Development Goals
authors: Priti Parikh; Loan Diep; Pascale Hofmann; Julia Tomei; Luiza C. Campos; Tse‐Hui Teh; Yacob Mulugetta; Ben M. Milligan
rationale: Although the record concerns sanitation services (C1), it is a macro-level SDG target-mapping study identifying cross-sectoral synergies and trade-offs between sanitation and the 169 UN SDG targets to justify strategic cross-sectoral investment in sanitation. It neither examines a legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff, tenure, or institutional mechanism governing sanitation access (failing C2, E03) nor measures household or community service access as an empirical outcome of such mechanisms (failing C4).

title: Women in Slum, Risking Their Safety to Access and Usage of Basic Sanitation Facilities-A Literature Review
authors: Ayush Prakash Hazare; Jyoti Jain Tholiya
rationale: Although the literature review addresses women's safe access to and usage of slum water and sanitation facilities (Criterion 1 and Criterion 4), the abstract explicitly specifies that the determinants analysed are physical and spatial infrastructure features—toilet block infrastructure, lighting, route, siting of public/community toilets, timings of use, and number of toilets—affecting exposure to crime and sexual violence. No legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or institutional governance mechanism is examined (E03: wrong exposure).

title: Sanitation challenges of the poor in urban and rural settings: Case studies of Bengaluru City and rural North Karnataka
authors: S. Manasi; Latha Nagesh; Hemalatha Ramesh
rationale: Empirical mixed-methods study (surveys of 400 slum residents in Bengaluru and 500 rural residents in North Karnataka plus FGDs and case studies) examining household/community toilet access, usage, and open defecation (C1, C3, C4 met). While the abstract highlights technical, behavioural, water-scarcity, cultural, space, and financial barriers alongside broad references to 'improved governance' and 'institutionalising the process of construction with transparency and accountability', full-text review is required under the narrow Criterion 2 reading to determine whether concrete administrative, subsidy-delivery, municipal O&M, or slum-tenure rules are empirically analysed rather than generic project delivery and behavioural factors.

title: Social Exclusion, Occupational Stigma, and Constrained Agency among Harijan Sanitation Workers in Urban Bangladesh: An Ethnographically Informed Case Study of the Ganaktuli Sweeper Colony, Dhaka
rationale: Although this qualitative ethnographic case study is empirical (c3 = yes) and mentions sanitation workers in Dhaka, its topic is occupational stigma, hereditary cleaning labour ("dirty work"), workplace harassment, institutional distance from general social-protection schemes, and constrained worker agency among Harijan municipal sweepers. It does not examine household or community access to water or sanitation services (c1 = no), legal/administrative mechanisms governing water or sanitation service access (c2 = no), or any water/sanitation service-access outcome (c4 = no). Excluded under E01 (wrong topic).

title: Water Insecurity and the Poor: Issues and Research Needs
rationale: Although the paper focuses on household water insecurity, clean water access, and high prices paid by the poor in developing countries (meeting C1 and C4), both the title ('Issues and Research Needs') and abstract make clear that this is a conceptual, narrative scoping paper elaborating a multidisciplinary framework, identifying knowledge gaps, and proposing a research agenda rather than reporting primary empirical evidence or a systematic review/meta-analysis (failing C3; excluded under E05).

title: The State of Brazilian Favelas: Infrastructural Regimes and Urban Inequality
authors: João Paulo Rodrigues da Silva; João Porto de Albuquerque; Júlio César Pedrassoli; Gabriel Spadon; Jose Fernando Rodrigues Junior
rationale: This empirical national-scale geospatial and census study measures household improved water and sanitation access across more than 12,000 Brazilian favelas (satisfying C1, C3, and C4), but fails Criterion 2 (E03: wrong exposure). The study explicitly integrates demographic, environmental, topographic, pollution, accessibility, and built-environment morphological variables to classify statistical 'infrastructural regimes' via unsupervised clustering and model socio-environmental correlates of service access, without examining any legal, administrative, tenure-rule, tariff, regulatory, or institutional governance mechanism.

title: Coordination: the key to governing the water-land-food nexus in Zambia?
rationale: Excluded under E07 (wrong service). The study examines cross-sectoral and vertical institutional coordination in Zambia's water-land-food nexus, specifically focusing on the expansion of agricultural irrigation and the planning and licensing of large-scale public-private agricultural investment projects rather than household or community drinking water or sanitation service access.

title: Making water affordable to all: A typology and evaluation of options for urban water pricing
rationale: The record clearly addresses urban household water supply access (C1), tariff/pricing design and administrative simplicity mechanisms (C2 narrow and plain), and affordability for poor customers (C4). However, the abstract frames the study as a 'typology of water pricing options' supported by a 'review of theoretical insights and empirical experiences,' leaving unclear whether it conducts a systematic empirical synthesis or primary/secondary empirical evaluation versus an unsystematic narrative/conceptual review (C3). Under Phase 5 rules against premature exclusion of tariff/affordability studies, full-text inspection is required ('unsure').

title: Making the Poor Pay for Public Goods via Microfinance: Economic and Political Pitfalls in the Case of Water and Sanitation
rationale: The study clearly addresses household water and sanitation service provision and equity/payment barriers for poor households in Vietnam and India (c1='yes', c4='yes'). However, full-text retrieval ('unsure') is required for two reasons: (1) under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, it is unclear from the abstract alone whether the two evaluated water/sanitation microfinance schemes operate through state, municipal, or utility cost-recovery, subsidy, tariff/connection-fee, or regulatory/institutional rules versus purely private microcredit lending (c2_legal_admin_narrow='unclear'); and (2) while two cases from Vietnam and India are 'presented and evaluated' with 'evidence' found, the abstract does not specify whether those case evaluations rely on primary empirical data or secondary conceptual/illustrative review (c3='unclear').

title: Evaluation de l’impact sur les ménages de la hausse du tarif de l’eau à Manaus (Brésil)
rationale: This empirical study evaluates a 31.51% municipal water tariff increase under an increasing block tariff (IBT) cross-subsidy structure in Manaus, Brazil, using a natural experiment comparing monthly household water consumption between 2003 and 2004. It clearly meets all eligibility criteria: household municipal water service (C1), a tariff and cross-subsidy pricing rule governing water access and affordability (C2 narrow and plain), quantitative empirical analysis (C3), and household water consumption quantity outcomes (C4).

title: Governing Pandemic Waterscapes: Covid-19 and Nairobi Metropolitan Services as Co-Catalysts of Waterscape Changes
authors: Sophie Schramm; Moritz Kasper; Emmanuel Mwenje; Simon Bohlen; Elizabeth Wamuchiru
rationale: The title and abstract clearly address urban household/community water access and equity outcomes in water-deprived areas of Nairobi (Criteria 1 and 4 met). Full-text retrieval is required ('unsure') for two reasons: (1) under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, examining Nairobi Metropolitan Services, changes in the city's overall governance structure, and pandemic water projects plausibly involves administrative/institutional restructuring, utility-governance rules, or emergency tariff/free-water mandates, though it could also be generic project delivery; and (2) the abstract does not explicitly state its empirical methodology (Criterion 3 unclear).

title: Decarbonizing the Food and Beverages Industry: A Critical and Systematic Review of Developments, Sociotechnical Systems and Policy Options
authors: Benjamin Kenneth Sovacool; Morgan Bazilian; Steve Griffiths; Jinsoo Kim; Aoife M Foley; David W. Rooney
rationale: Excluded under E01 (wrong topic). This systematic review examines greenhouse gas emissions, energy/carbon footprints, and decarbonization technologies and policies in the food and beverage industry. Aside from a passing background mention of industrial/supply-chain water consumption as an environmental impact of food and beverage consumption, it does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (Criterion 1) or water/sanitation access outcomes (Criterion 4).

title: Private Sector Participation in the Water and Wastewater Services Industry
rationale: This 2004 paper examines private sector participation (privatization, greenfield projects, concessions, leases, operation and management contracts and outsourcing) in the water and wastewater utilities sector, noting customer service improvements alongside social and economic concerns tied to water as a basic human necessity, as well as global trade and investment patterns. Because utility ownership and concession/contractual structures are squarely within scope of Criterion 2, and the unstructured abstract does not make clear whether the full text contains empirical analysis/case-study data (c3) measuring household water/sanitation access, coverage or affordability outcomes (c4) versus a non-empirical trade/market overview, the protocol rule against prematurely excluding ambiguous utility-governance abstracts requires an 'unsure' verdict for full-text retrieval.

title: MWSS Privatization: Implications on the Price of Water, the Poor and the Environment
rationale: This study clearly meets (or strongly appears to meet) all Phase 5 Title/Abstract inclusion criteria. C1 is satisfied because it focuses on urban household water supply and sewerage services in Metro Manila, including tap connections, shared connections and public faucets. C2 (both narrow and plain) is satisfied because it analyses MWSS utility privatization, specific provisions, performance targets and coverage exceptions in the MWSS concession agreement, and the progressive water tariff structure. C3 is satisfied at Title/Abstract stage because the paper conducts quantitative/socio-legal empirical and demand-projection analysis of service coverage, concession targets and water pricing (with full-text review to confirm the exact balance of primary empirical data versus demand projections). C4 is satisfied because it evaluates service coverage, water rationing/shortages and regressive affordability impacts on poor households paying higher prices via shared connections, public faucets and private water markets.

title: The Failure of Public Water Utility Privatization From Araral’s Perspective: Implications for Ethiopia’s Water Sector
rationale: Although the topic concerns public water utility privatization and institutional reform (satisfying Criterion 1 and Criterion 2 under both narrow and plain readings), the abstract explicitly shows that this piece is a critical commentary/review of a single published paper by Professor Eduardo Araral ("The Failure of Water Utilities Privatization: Synthesis of Evidence, Analysis and Implications"), examining "the limitations of the article, and the implication for the Ethiopian water utility sector." It presents neither primary empirical data collection nor a systematic empirical synthesis/meta-analysis, failing Criterion 3 (E05).

title: Universal access to drinking water: the role of aid
authors: Robert Bain; Rolf Luyendijk; Jamie Bartram
rationale: Although the study empirically evaluates progress toward universal drinking water access across developing countries (meeting C1, C3, and C4), its exposure of interest is macro-level water sector spending and the aggregate volume of international development aid rather than a legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff/subsidy rule, tenure, enforcement, or institutional mechanism governing service access (failing Criterion 2; E03 wrong exposure).

title: Private Sector Involvement in Water Services: Theoretical Foundations and Empirical Evidence
authors: María Á. García-Valiñas; Francisco Gonzales; Javier de Andrés Suárez; Vera Zaporozhets
rationale: The study empirically estimates the impact of public-private partnerships (contracting-out/privatization) and concession reservation prices in Spanish municipal urban water supply (satisfying C1, C2 narrow and plain, and C3). However, the abstract frames outcomes around local government debt reduction and 'water price increases' without specifying whether residential household water bills, affordability burdens, or household access/disconnection outcomes are analysed versus aggregate utility price/revenue indices. Full-text review is required to verify Criterion 4 eligibility.

title: Neither Private nor Public: The Effects of Communal Provision of Water on Child Health in Peru
rationale: This quantitative empirical study (2006-2010 household- and child-level survey data in Peru using an IV strategy) examines household/municipal water service provision under communal/cooperative utility governance (Comités Vecinales and Juntas Administrativas de Servicios de Saneamiento, instrumented via municipal personnel resources and administrative urban/rural classification; keywords include 'water utilities, cooperatives, child health, regulation, Peru'). Criteria 1, 2 (both narrow utility-ownership/regulatory-structure and plain institutional/governance), and 3 are satisfied. However, the title and abstract report only child health ('diarrhea among under- five year old children') as the outcome; full-text retrieval is required to determine whether intermediate or secondary water service-access outcomes (such as household connection, coverage, continuity, chlorination/service quality, or affordability) are also empirically analysed (Criterion 4).

title: The Impact of Institutional Frameworks on Private Sector Participation in Water Supply and Sanitation: The case of the management contract for water and wastewater services in the Amman Governorate, Jordan
rationale: This empirical field case study investigates the Management Contract for Water and Wastewater Services in Amman, Jordan, examining how specific contract rules, regulatory institutions, and judicial checks constrain or enable discretionary behaviour in operating a municipal water and wastewater utility (meeting Criteria 1, 2 narrow/plain, and 3). However, the abstract refers generally to the 'outcome of the PSP arrangement' and 'performance of a privately operated water utility' without specifying whether household- or user-facing service access outcomes (such as supply continuity, coverage, connection, reliability, or affordability) are measured alongside contractual/managerial indicators. Full-text review is therefore required to verify Criterion 4.

title: Nature-Based Solutions in Coastal Governance, A Legal Analysis of Beach Concession Contracts in Mar del Plata, Argentina
authors: Cecilia Lucía Mantecón; Clara María Minaverry
rationale: Exclude (E01 - wrong topic). This study conducts an environmental-law and content analysis of 36 municipal tender specifications for commercial beach tourist concessions (Fiscal Tourist Units) in Mar del Plata, Argentina, focusing on coastal adaptation, aquifer protection, water-efficiency clauses, and Nature-Based Solutions. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (fails Criterion 1) or any household/community water or sanitation access outcome (fails Criterion 4).

title: The link between water access and subjective well-being: some methods and proposals
authors: Francisco González‐Gómez; Jorge Guardiola; Teresa García‐Muñoz
rationale: This conceptual and methodological paper offers research proposals and methodological notes on investigating how water access affects subjective well-being (happiness). It presents no empirical primary data or systematic synthesis (E05), reverses the causal direction of interest (treating water access as a predictor of subjective well-being rather than an access outcome), and does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access beyond noting potential relevance to human-rights framing and NGO/government decision-making.

title: The political economy of the peruvian urban water sector
rationale: This mixed-methods study investigates regulation and political economy in the Peruvian urban water sector using qualitative analysis and quantitative tests of political budget cycles, partisan effects and the median voter theorem. Because the abstract is written as a structural section overview without specifying the exact regulatory/tariff/utility-governance mechanisms or whether the empirical outcomes measure household water access, coverage, service continuity/quality or tariff affordability (versus purely fiscal or budgetary aggregates), full-text review is required; premature exclusion of an ambiguous urban water utility regulation and governance study is unwarranted.

title: An assessment of a novel franchise model for addressing the challenge of sustainable water access in resource-poor settings
authors: Martin Muchangi; Daniel Kurao; Kennedy Omwaka; Kioko Kithuki; Tara Klijn; Maarten Kuijpers; Gilbert Wangalwa; Kimani Karuga
rationale: Mixed-methods empirical evaluation (n=1,209 household surveys, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions across five pilot sites in Kajiado County, Kenya) of the WaterStarters franchise model for drinking water access, measuring safe, affordable, and reliable household water outcomes. Criteria 1, 3, and 4 are clearly satisfied. Under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, the abstract plausibly implicates utility-ownership/franchise governance and tariff/cost-recovery/hybrid-financing rules affecting affordability and access, but could alternatively focus on NGO project delivery and commercial return; therefore full-text review is required (unsure).

title: The ambiguous infrastructural ideal: the urbanisation of water and power in the 'golden age' of utility networks
rationale: The abstract addresses urban water (and power) network rollout, service universalization and socio-spatial fragmentation ('splintering') across four historical urban case studies (Rome, Cape Town, Paris and Los Angeles), examining public versus private utility ownership, unbundling, governance frameworks and regulation. Full-text review is required to determine (1) whether the historical case studies report primary empirical/archival evidence rather than a purely conceptual or secondary synthesis, and (2) under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, whether specific utility-ownership or regulatory mechanisms governing water service access are analysed rather than macro-level urban regime background alone.

title: Toward the adaptation to new regulation on water pricing in the agricultural sector: a case study from northern Italy
authors: Francesco Galioto; Elisa Guerra; Meri Raggi; Davide Viaggi
rationale: Excluded under E07 (wrong service). The study models Water Framework Directive agricultural water-pricing rules applied by Reclamation and Irrigation Boards in northern Italy, focusing entirely on agricultural irrigation water demand, crop yields, irrigation technology adoption, and farm profits rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.

title: Reality Versus Propaganda in the Formation of Beliefs About Privatization
authors: Rafael Di Tella; Sebastián Galiani; Ernesto Schargrodsky
rationale: Although the paper is set in the context of Argentina's privatization and 2006 re-nationalization of water services and compares respondents who gained water access with those who did not, water access is an explanatory variable rather than an outcome. The study empirically examines the formation of public beliefs and opinions about privatization (measured on a 1-10 scale) in response to first-hand experience of utility investment versus priming with government propaganda, clearly failing Criterion 4 (wrong outcome, E04).

title: Water Markets in Mexico: Opportunities and Constraints
rationale: Excluded under E07 (wrong service). The paper examines Mexico's 1992 Federal Water Law and market transfers of water-use concessions/permits among agricultural irrigators, focusing on irrigation management, irrigators' water-use efficiency, and bulk water resource allocation rather than household or community drinking water or sanitation service access.

title: The Right to Dignity and Sanitation for Manual Scavengers' Children: Examining Access to Education and Healthcare in India’s Informal Communities
rationale: Excluded (primary code E07: wrong service; also fails C2 narrow, C3, and C4). Although the title invokes the right to dignity and sanitation in India's informal communities, the abstract explicitly states that the article focuses on the limited access to education and healthcare of children of manual scavengers (sanitation workers), treating poor sanitation only as one background hardship affecting children's educational and health prospects rather than examining household or community water or sanitation service access outcomes. Moreover, the legal discussion centres on prohibitions against manual scavenging labour rather than rules governing water/sanitation service access, and the abstract describes a purely normative/doctrinal essay arguing for a multi-sectoral policy approach with no primary empirical data or systematic review methodology.

title: Sanitation for Sustainable Development in Informal Settlements in Kigali City, Rwanda: A Synthesis of the Evidence To Inform Policy and Practice
rationale: The paper addresses liquid and solid waste sanitation access for residents of informal settlements in Kigali, Rwanda (c1 = yes, c4 = yes). However, full-text review is required on two grounds: (1) under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, it is unclear whether the analysis of informal settlements, public funding, and the Kigali masterplan of 2020 examines specific legal, planning/tenure, regulatory, or subsidy/financing rules rather than general infrastructure shortfalls and local awareness; and (2) under Criterion 3, it is unclear whether the 'in-depth discussions among urban governance stakeholders' and 'review of the literature' represent systematic qualitative empirical data or a narrative policy-community synthesis. Per Phase 5 protocol rules against prematurely excluding ambiguous informal-settlement governance abstracts, the record is retained as unsure.

title: The Impact of Kenya's Affordable Housing Programme: A Case Study of Mukuru Kwa Njenga Informal Settlement
rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study (n=140 households, semi-structured interviews, and document review) evaluates Kenya's Affordable Housing Programme (AHP) in the Mukuru Kwa Njenga informal settlement and compares it with Kenya's Informal Settlements Improvement Programme (KISIP). Although the primary intervention is housing (raising potential E07 wrong-service exclusion), the abstract explicitly reports significant improvements in household sanitation and service reliability and finds that programme access is gated by administrative barriers—specifically digital registration and documentation requirements—alongside strained payment obligations. Full-text review is required to determine whether sanitation and water service access/reliability are substantively measured and linked to these administrative/documentation rules (or KISIP upgrading), or mentioned solely as peripheral components of general housing satisfaction.

title: Azerbaijan: Water Supply & Sanitation in Secondary Towns
rationale: The record clearly concerns municipal household water supply and sanitation access, reliability, and affordability in 52 secondary towns in Azerbaijan (C1 and C4 met). It explicitly includes an examination of the legislative and institutional framework, SuKanal utility structures, and financial/affordability dimensions alongside reconnaissance-level surveys in 13 towns and feasibility studies in 3 towns, paired with a prospective 10-year spreadsheet investment model. Full-text retrieval is required ('unsure') to determine whether the report presents empirical socio-legal/institutional evidence linking regulatory, utility-governance, or tariff/cost-recovery mechanisms to service access outcomes, or whether the legislative/institutional section is purely descriptive background to an ex-ante capital-investment simulation.

title: Assessment of Informal Settlement in Central Kandahar: A Case Study of Area Within Four Historic Gateways
rationale: This mixed-methods empirical case study examines squatter settlements and informal subdivisions in central Kandahar and explicitly includes 'Limited Basic Services' and 'Inadequate Sanitation Facilities' among the assessed ramifications of informal settlements, alongside references to urban planning policy. However, from the abstract alone it is unclear whether water/sanitation access is substantively measured rather than mentioned among general living-condition indicators, and whether legal tenure status, formal recognition, or municipal planning rules governing service provision are analysed. Under Phase 5 rules against prematurely excluding ambiguous informal-settlement abstracts, full-text retrieval is required ('unsure').

title: Local Election and Water Tariff Revision: Evidence from Japan
authors: Sasamori, Sanae; Komatsuzaki, Shunsaku; Kato, Hironori
rationale: This empirical political-economy paper analyses Japanese municipal water utilities to test how mayoral and local assembly election cycles, existing tariff rates, and utility financial health affect the probability and extent of utility water tariff revisions. Water tariff revision is the dependent variable (framed as balancing political timing with financially driven utility management) rather than an exposure governing household access, and the study measures no household or community water access, connection, coverage, availability, continuity, quality, consumer affordability, or disconnection/exclusion outcome (E04 wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2).

title: Addressing Blind Spots through the Water-Sanitation-Climate Nexus
rationale: This title and abstract describe a purely conceptual/theoretical paper proposing the 'Water-Sanitation-Climate nexus' as an integrated analytical framework for climate mitigation and macro water-sanitation resource interactions. It presents no empirical primary study or systematic review (E05), examines no legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff, or tenure mechanism governing water or sanitation access, and measures no household or community service-access outcomes.

title: Assessment of Factors Impacting Water Supply Services in Lusaka District: A Case of Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company
rationale: Although this qualitative expert-interview case study of Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company (LWSC) addresses urban household water supply access, availability, and continuity (C1=yes, C3=yes, C4=yes), it fails Criterion 2 under the active narrow rule-type reading (C2_narrow=no, E03). The abstract explicitly defines both the analytical focus and findings around environmental, demographic, and physical source-water stressors—climate change (droughts and erratic rainfall), rapid population growth straining infrastructure capacity, and unplanned land development causing groundwater pollution in shallow water tables—rather than legal, regulatory, tariff, tenure/documentation, enforcement, or administrative rules governing household water access.

title: Drinking Water, Sanitation, and Health in India: Policy Framework, Challenges and Opportunities
rationale: The record clearly addresses household/population drinking water and sanitation access in India (c1 = yes) and describes disparities in access to water sources, water quantity/quality, and sanitation facilities alongside health and macroeconomic impacts (c4 = yes). However, two criteria are ambiguous from the title and abstract alone and require full-text verification: (1) c2_legal_admin_narrow is 'unclear' because references to 'Policy Framework', 'multiple modes and models of water provisioning', and 'major government policies promulgated in recent years' could encompass utility/institutional provisioning structures, regulatory frameworks, or tariff/subsidy rules, or could instead be limited to unanalysed macro-policy/program overviews; and (2) c3_empirical_or_systematic_review is 'unclear' because 'This chapter does a comprehensive analysis of these challenges' may rely on empirical analysis of household survey/secondary data (common in Indian water governance chapters) or may be a non-empirical narrative overview chapter. Per Phase 5 rules against premature exclusion of ambiguous governance abstracts, the verdict is 'unsure'.

title: Threshold Tight, Prices Light: Nonlinear Tariff Design and Household Water Conservation
authors: Li, Li; Li, Jun; Jeuland, Marc
rationale: This empirical study examines domestic water tariff structure (increasing block tariffs vs. flat-rate tariffs, focusing on block quantity threshold tightness and price gaps) among households in Hangzhou, China, satisfying Criterion 1 (household water service), Criterion 2 under both narrow and plain readings (tariff design), and Criterion 3 (empirical stated-preference and baseline household survey evidence). However, the study is framed around demand conservation and willingness to adopt water-saving technologies in hypothetical stated-preference IBT scenarios, while also reporting reductions in annual household water consumption and testing 'unfavorable bill assessments' (a plausible affordability/bill-burden indicator) alongside baseline IBT vs. flat-rate exposure. Full-text retrieval ('unsure') is required to verify whether the study reports eligible household water access, essential-quantity, or affordability outcomes rather than purely hypothetical behavioral conservation intentions.

title: Quantifying Water and Sanitation in Development Cooperation: Power or Perversity?
rationale: While the paper addresses domestic water and sanitation in international development cooperation (c1 = yes), it is a critical/conceptual historical essay examining global quantitative target setting (1976 onward, the MDGs, and post-2015 measurement options) rather than an empirical primary study or systematic review (c3 = no, E05). It also neither examines a legal or administrative rule mechanism governing household/community service access under narrow Criterion 2 (c2_narrow = no) nor evaluates empirical water/sanitation access outcomes (c4 = no).

title: Enhanced Local Contractor Participation: Case of Zambia Water Supply and Sanitation Sub-Sector
rationale: Excluded (E01): This study examines industrial/procurement barriers to local construction contractor participation and competitiveness in public infrastructure tenders in Zambia's water and sanitation construction sub-sector. Its population is construction contractors and its target outcome is local contractor involvement in infrastructure procurement rather than household or community water or sanitation service access, coverage, reliability, affordability, or exclusion.

title: Investigating Factors Affecting Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Practices on Chilwa Islands
rationale: Mixed-methods primary study of WASH challenges on Chilwa Island, Zambia. Although it touches on household/community water access and sanitation infrastructure (C1, C4) using empirical survey and interview data (C3), its explicit exposure scope is socio-economic, cultural, and environmental factors shaping WASH practices rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or institutional mechanism governing service access (fails C2; exclude under E03).

title: Efficiency Effects of 'Privatization' in Argentina's Water and Sanitation Services
rationale: Although the study examines water and sanitation sector privatization and incentive-based regulatory regimes in Argentina using empirical upper-bound estimates for four private operators, its outcome is strictly firm-level economic efficiency gains and regulatory accounting data processes. Neither the title nor the abstract indicates any evaluation of household or community water or sanitation access, coverage, connections, continuity, quality or affordability (failing Criterion 4, E04).

title: Neighborhood Sanitation and Infant Mortality
rationale: This empirical health/development economics paper investigates the Hindu-Muslim infant mortality puzzle in India, showing that neighborhood sanitation externalities explain why children in Muslim neighborhoods have higher survival to age one. It does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or institutional mechanism governing sanitation service access (failing Criterion 2 under both narrow and plain readings, E03), and its primary outcome is infant mortality rather than water/sanitation service access (failing Criterion 4).

title: Expanding Access to Clean Water for the Rural Poor: Experimental Evidence from Malawi
authors: Dupas, Pascaline; Nhlema, Basimenye; Wagner, Zachary; Wolf, Aaron; Wroe, Emily
rationale: This 18-month randomized controlled trial in Malawi evaluates a public-health program providing monthly coupons for free point-of-use water treatment solution (diluted chlorine) versus routine household distribution and promotion by Community Health Workers (CHWs). Even if household water purification is treated as borderline on water service access (C1 unclear, C4 yes), the study clearly fails the narrow rule-type Criterion 2 reading (E03 wrong exposure): it tests health-product delivery channels (coupons vs CHW visits) and behavioural promotion for bottled chlorine rather than any legal, regulatory, tenure/documentation, utility tariff/subsidy, disconnection, or formal administrative mechanism governing household or community water/sanitation service access.

title: Imperfect Competition and Sanitation: Evidence from Randomized Auctions in Senegal
authors: Houde, Jean-François; Johnson, Terence; Lipscomb, Molly; Schechter, Laura
rationale: The study empirically examines household sanitation access (latrine desludging prices and counterfactual take-up of improved sanitation technology in Dakar, Senegal; C1=yes, C3=yes, C4=yes). However, under the narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, the exposure studied is private-sector imperfect competition/bidder collusion (including informal/private price coordination by a trade association) and researcher-randomized design features in an experimental auction platform, rather than a legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, public tariff/subsidy, bureaucratic discretion, enforcement/disconnection, or utility-regulatory mechanism (C2_narrow=no; E03 wrong exposure).

title: Privatization of Public Goods: Evidence from the Sanitation Sector in Senegal
authors: Deutschmann, Joshua; Gars, Jared; Houde, Jean-François; Lipscomb, Molly; Schechter, Laura
rationale: Empirical quantitative study in Dakar, Senegal examining the privatization of sewage treatment center management (a utility/infrastructure ownership and governance mechanism) using administrative records (2009-2018), household survey data, and DHS data, measuring household sanitation service prices (affordability) and legal sanitary waste dumping volumes. Meets all inclusion criteria (C1-C4).

title: Information and Modeling Issues in Designing Water and Sanitation Subsidy Schemes
authors: Gomez-Lobo, Andres; Foster, Vivien; Halpern, Jonathan
rationale: The record clearly concerns household water and sanitation service access (C1 = yes) and explicitly examines a core administrative/regulatory tariff-and-subsidy mechanism—specifically eligibility criteria, targeting properties, formal versus informal customer coverage, and administrative costs in designing Panama's water subsidy proposal (C2 narrow = yes; C2 plain = yes). However, because the title and abstract frame the paper around methodological data-collation and spreadsheet simulation modeling issues for an ex-ante subsidy proposal, full-text inspection is required to determine whether the paper reports primary empirical analysis of household/utility data on service affordability, targeting, or exclusion outcomes (C3 = unclear; C4 = unclear) rather than a purely methodological or hypothetical simulation discussion.

title: Water and Sanitation Services for Informal Settlements in Honiara, Solomon Islands
rationale: The study examines water and sanitation service access, safety, and affordability for residents of informal settlements in Honiara served or targeted by the public utility Solomon Water (c1 = yes, c4 = yes). Utility service expansion into informal settlements plausibly examines tenure/documentation barriers, tariff/affordability rules, or utility regulatory mandates under the narrow Criterion 2 reading (c2_legal_admin_narrow = unclear), and clearly involves institutional service-delivery governance under the plain reading (c2_legal_admin_plain = yes). Because the abstract notes 'input from Solomon Water, informal settlement residents and other stakeholders, together with analytical information' without detailing whether systematic primary empirical research is reported versus a policy options consultancy assessment (c3 = unclear), full-text review is required ('unsure').

title: Papua New Guinea : Sanitation, Water Supply and Hygiene in Urban Informal Settlements
rationale: This 2014 World Bank WSP empirical study examines household/community water supply and sanitation access, service coverage gaps, affordability, and barriers in urban informal settlements in Port Moresby and Wewak, Papua New Guinea (meeting Criteria 1, 3, and 4). Because World Bank WSP informal-settlement WASH barrier assessments frequently examine land tenure/informality restrictions, utility service-area mandates, and tariff/connection-cost barriers—especially when framed around a draft National WASH Policy—but the abstract does not explicitly specify which barriers are analyzed, the record is retained as 'unsure' for full-text verification under Phase 5 informal-settlement screening rules.

title: Water Supply and Sanitation (WSS): Strengthening Climate-Informed Project Design
rationale: Although the record concerns extending water supply and sanitation services to unserved or underserved segments (C1/C4), its exposure is climate-informed project design and technical/operational investments (energy efficiency, nonrevenue water reduction, climate resilience, and demand-side efficiency) rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff, tenure, or utility-governance rule or mechanism (failing C2; generic project delivery is expressly out of scope). Excluded under E03 (wrong exposure).

title: Building Partnerships for Sustainable Water and Sanitation Services in Africa
rationale: Although the record broadly concerns water and sanitation services in Africa (C1), it is an institutional briefing note providing a rapid scan of inter-donor partnership activities (operational cooperation, information sharing, capacity-building training, and results monitoring) among the World Bank, AfDB, and WSP. It neither presents empirical primary research or a systematic review (failing C3, E05) nor examines legal, regulatory, or administrative rules governing household/community water or sanitation access outcomes (failing C2 and C4).

title: Water and sanitation to reduce child mortality: The impact and cost of water and sanitation infrastructure
rationale: Although this empirical study involves household water and sanitation infrastructure (c1 = yes, c3 = yes), it treats improved water and sanitation access as the exposure/explanatory variable to estimate child mortality reductions and macro cost-effectiveness (cost per life-year saved relative to GDP per capita). It does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff or governance mechanism governing access (failing Criterion 2; E03) nor does it evaluate determinants of household service access as an outcome (failing Criterion 4; E04).
